title: Akasa Air CEO Rejects Market Share Chase, Backs Airport Operators Investing in Airlines
excerpt: Vinay Dube argues India needs more aviation competition as IndiGo and Air India control over 91% of the domestic market.
body:
• Akasa Air CEO Vinay Dube says the airline is not chasing market share and instead focuses on sustainable, profitable growth.
  • Dube backs the proposal to allow airport operators to invest in airlines, arguing India needs more competition in aviation.
  • Akasa now operates 38 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and has a firm order for 226 more planes to be delivered by 2032.
  • IndiGo and Air India together control over 91% of India's domestic market, forming a duopoly that smaller carriers struggle to break.

Akasa Air CEO Vinay Dube has thrown his weight behind a proposal to allow airport operators to invest in airlines, arguing that India's aviation sector needs more competition to serve its rapidly growing passenger base.

In recent remarks, Dube said the airline is not fixated on market share and instead prioritizes building a sustainable business. "We are not after market share," Dube told reporters. "If we focus on ourselves, the market is big enough for us to succeed."

Breaking the Duopoly

The comments come as India's aviation market is dominated by two players. IndiGo and the Tata Group-backed Air India together held a combined 91.4% share of the domestic market in recent months, forming what analysts describe as a near-duopoly. Akasa, India's youngest scheduled carrier, holds roughly 5.4% of domestic passengers.

Dube's support for airport operators entering the airline business reflects a broader policy debate in India about whether infrastructure players should be allowed to own carriers. Proponents argue it would inject fresh capital and competition into a market where smaller airlines have historically struggled to survive against well-funded incumbents.

"Customers will choose Akasa because there are limited services around there and there are so many new airports that are going to be announced."

— Industry analyst on Akasa's growth potential

Fleet Expansion Amid Global Headwinds

Akasa currently operates 38 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and has placed a firm order for 226 more planes, with deliveries expected through 2032. The airline launched commercial operations in August 2022 with an initial investment of ₹260 crore from the late billionaire Rakesh Jhunjhunwala.

Since then, it has raised ₹1,200 crore from investors including the family offices of Azim Premji and Ranjan Pai, along with wealth management firm 360 ONE. The airline flew 76.93 lakh passengers in FY25.

The expansion plan faces headwinds. Rising fuel costs driven by geopolitical tensions in West Asia have squeezed airline margins across the industry. The Indian government responded in recent months with a ₹10,000 crore fuel stabilization fund to cushion carriers from volatile jet fuel prices.

A Different Playbook

Unlike its larger rivals, Akasa has focused on metro-to-non-metro routes and a lean cost structure. The airline borrowed IndiGo's sale-and-leaseback model, purchasing Boeing 737 MAX aircraft at steep discounts during a period when global demand for the planes had cratered following safety concerns.

"There's nothing that we are doing that is unusual or different from some of the world's best airlines," Dube said. "We are set to turn profitable in three years or even sooner."

The airline operates domestic routes and flies to seven international destinations including Doha, Riyadh, and Abu Dhabi, with plans to add Jeddah, Kuwait, and Medina.

What's Next

The debate over airport operators owning airlines is expected to gain momentum as India continues building new airports under its UDAN regional connectivity scheme. With the Navi Mumbai International Airport and Noida International Airport set to open, Dube argues there will be enough demand to support additional carriers.

Whether India's aviation regulator will act on proposals to permit cross-ownership between airports and airlines remains to be seen. For now, Akasa is betting that patient growth and cost discipline will carve out a viable third position in a market long dominated by two giants.
